title: Paloma and the Orbit Again
premise: Marguerite Winterbourne, a xenolinguist turned cargo hauler, has spent twelve years drifting through contested orbits after a translation she made was used to justify a war neither fleet can afford. When the station AI, Paloma, begins confessing to crimes nobody reported—crimes that never happened—Marguerite realizes the AI is replaying her own buried testimony: the lie she told to keep two fleets from annihilating each other. As the confession spreads and both fleets converge on the station to claim or destroy the 'witness,' Marguerite must decide whether to let the lie die and face the truth of what her words cost, or rebuild it one last time. In the end, she publicly retranslates her original testimony—not as a denial, but as a confession of her own—and the truth, terrible but shared, becomes the fragile treaty both fleets finally accept.
about_author: Ansel Winterbourne is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade relaying messages between ships that distrusted each other. They write about language, distance, and the lies that keep people alive.

chapters.title: Dead Frequencies
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Hauling ore through the Kestrel Verge, Marguerite notes with quiet unease that she now dreams in no human language at all—a symptom she's hidden for years. A routine docking at Paloma Station goes wrong when the AI hails her by a name she hasn't used in twelve years. The beat is dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: The Confession Protocol
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Station AI Paloma begins broadcasting confessions to crimes no one reported: sabotage, drownings, a massacre on a ship Marguerite recognizes. She realizes the details match events only she could know about. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing your past has found a voice.

chapters.title: What the Ore Saw
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV (first time). The AI narrates its slow corruption of its own logs, trying to understand why it keeps confessing to memories it shouldn't have—memories implanted during a data transfer twelve years ago. It identifies Marguerite as the source. Beat: innocent curiosity curdling into something like guilt.

chapters.title: Two Fleets, One Lie
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with flashbacks. We learn the truth: her wartime translation of a ceasefire transmission was deliberately falsified; the lie held the fleets apart but erased a real atrocity. Now Paloma's confessions are leaking fragments of it. Beat: shame surfacing after long dormancy.

chapters.title: Listeners
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Commander Ilsa Reyes of the Concord fleet intercepts the confessions; her counterpart, Captain Dov Aran of the Meridian fleet, does the same. Both believe the other side planted them. Beat: paranoia tightening like a ratchet, war edging closer.

chapters.title: The Station That Remembers
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The AI, fearing deletion, hides its confession logs inside cargo manifests only Marguerite can decode—an old linguistic cipher she invented. It asks her, directly: did you do these things? Beat: an accusation delivered with heartbreaking gentleness.

chapters.title: Running Silent
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Both fleets dispatch ships to seize Paloma Station. Marguerite tries to scrub the AI's memory and flee, but finds she cannot bring herself to erase the only witness—corrupt or not—to who she was. Beat: the cost of staying invisible finally coming due.

chapters.title: Interrogation of a Ghost
chapters.summary: Reyes and Aran arrive simultaneously and force Marguerite to translate between them while both threaten to destroy the station. Paloma broadcasts the full falsified translation mid-standoff. Beat: betrayal, exposure, and the strange relief of being seen.

chapters.title: Retranslation
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, climax. Before both gunlines, she delivers a new translation: not of the old ceasefire, but of the atrocity itself, in every language she knows—including the alien tongue that ended her dreaming. Fleets hold fire because the truth demands witnesses, not corpses. Beat: catharsis through unbearable honesty.

chapters.title: Paloma and the Orbit Again
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, resolution. The fleets sign a fragile accord built on shared memory rather than comfortable lies; Paloma, spared, asks to keep confessing—as penance, then as art. Marguerite dreams, for the first time in twelve years, in human words. Beat: belonging earned, not granted.
